The Lord is my helper and my protector; in Him my heart hoped, and I was helped, and my flesh blossomed anew; from my own will I will thank Him.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: conditional oath invoking loss if guilty
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The psalmist's preceding if-clauses deny injustice and wrongful repayment, then invoke pursuit, trampling and glory in dust if the condition is true. Job similarly tests his innocence and invokes loss of his harvest and rootedness if he has turned aside or touched gifts. Both speakers support a claim of innocence by calling down a concrete adverse consequence upon themselves if guilty, with different offenses and penalties.

final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The psalm repeats advice to move to the mountains like a little bird amid the following threat from armed sinners. David describes the king seeking his soul as the night-raven pursues in the mountains. Both use a bird-and-mountains comparison within danger or pursuit, but the psalm's bird is told to flee and Samuel's night-raven pursues. This literary comparison neither identifies the birds nor establishes Saul's pursuit as the psalm's occasion.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: For the end. A psalm of David. In the Lord I have trusted. How will you say to my soul, “Move away to the mountains like a little bird”?

target_units.text: Now let my blood not fall to the ground opposite the Lord’s presence. Israel’s king has come out to seek my soul, as the night-raven pursues in the mountains.”

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: hope of divine appearance linked with moral conduct
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The psalmist anticipates appearing before God's face in righteousness and being satisfied when His glory appears. John joins the hope of seeing Him when manifested with purifying oneself. Both connect hoped-for encounter with the divine presence to moral conduct; John's likeness to Him and the psalm's satisfaction remain distinct, and resurrection or awakening is not added to the psalm's wording.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: But I, in righteousness, will appear before Thy face; I will be satisfied when Thy glory appears.

target_units.text: Beloved, we are children of God now, and what we will be has not yet been manifested. We know that when He is manifested we will be like Him, because we will see Him as He is.
And everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as He is pure.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: contrast between downfall and being raised
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The psalm contrasts their being fettered and falling with our rising and being set upright, in the context of trust in the Lord rather than chariots and horses. Proverbs contrasts the righteous person's repeated falling and rising with the impious becoming weak amid evils. Both express a contrast through falling and rising, without identifying the psalm's opponents or importing the proverb's seven falls into its scene.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: They were fettered and fell, but we rose and were set upright.

target_units.text: for the righteous will fall seven times and rise, but the impious will grow weak amid evils.

final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The Lord teaches the meek His ways and guides them in judgment. James directs readers to receive the implanted word with gentleness and become its doers. Both connect a gentle disposition with receiving instruction that governs conduct; the psalm describes the Lord's teaching and James addresses the hearer's response, without equating every detail of their respective instruction.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: He will guide the meek in judgment; He will teach the meek His ways.

target_units.text: Therefore, putting away every impurity and the abundance of evil, receive with gentleness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
But become doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: hostile oppression portrayed as eating flesh
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The psalm portrays evildoers approaching to eat the speaker's flesh. Micah addresses unjust authorities through the image of stripping and eating the flesh of God's people. Both make devouring human flesh an image of hostile violence or oppression; Micah names corrupt authorities, while the psalm leaves its attackers unnamed and separately reports their collapse.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: When those doing evil approached me to eat my flesh, those who afflict me and my enemies, they grew weak and fell.

final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The psalm joins the lifting of the speaker's head above enemies to sacrifice and promised song to the Lord. David's song in Samuel joins being lifted above attackers and rescued to acknowledging the Lord and singing praise. The shared sequence is deliverance above hostile people followed by praise; Samuel does not supply the psalm's tent sacrifice or identify its occasion.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: bodily renewal joined with prayer and thanksgiving
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The psalmist credits the Lord's help with flesh blossoming anew and answers with willing thanks. Elihu describes the Lord renewing a sufferer's body, softening the flesh like an infant's, accepting prayer and rescuing life for praise. Both associate bodily renewal with divine help and a worshipful response. Elihu's conditional account and confession of blame are not imposed upon the psalmist, and no common healing episode is claimed.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: The Lord is my helper and my protector; in Him my heart hoped, and I was helped, and my flesh blossomed anew; from my own will I will thank Him.

target_units.text: He will hold him back from falling into death, and renew his body like plaster upon a wall, and fill his bones with marrow;
He will soften his flesh like an infant’s and restore him, grown to manhood, among humans.
When he prays to the Lord, it will be acceptable to Him; he will enter with a pure face, with confession, and He will return righteousness to humans.
Then the human will blame himself, saying, ‘What things I carried through! He did not examine me as my sins deserved.
Save my soul from coming into corruption, and my life will see light.’
Behold, the Strong One works all these things in three ways with a man.
But He rescued my soul from death, so that my life might praise Him in light.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: ethical contrast concerning joy at an enemy's distress
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The lament complains that opponents rejoiced and gathered against the speaker amid his trouble. Proverbs prohibits rejoicing or exalting oneself when an enemy falls, because the Lord sees and disapproves. The comparison concerns malicious delight in another's distress; it does not paraphrase the psalm's difficult clauses about gathered scourges and being torn apart, or identify its enemies.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: But against me they rejoiced and gathered; scourges gathered against me, and I did not know; they were torn apart and felt no remorse.

target_units.text: If your enemy falls, do not rejoice over him, and at his tripping do not lift yourself up,
for the Lord will see, and it will not please Him, and He will turn His wrath away from him.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: readiness for bodily scourging in contrasting voices
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The psalmist says he is ready for scourges with pain continually before him. Isaiah's speaker gives his back to scourges while refusing to disobey the Lord's instruction and trusting His help. Both expressly describe readiness to face bodily blows, but the psalm's surrounding confession of lawlessness and Isaiah's declaration of obedience remain distinct; the speakers and their occasions are not identified.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: For I am ready for scourges, and my pain is continually before me.
